shots.text: It is May, nineteen eighteen.
At a railway station in Russia, a train carrying former prisoners of war passes a group of Czech and Slovak soldiers.
Someone throws a piece of iron from a carriage.
It strikes a legionary, seriously injuring him.
His comrades stop the train, find the man they believe responsible, and kill him.
Local Bolshevik authorities arrest several of the soldiers.
Their comrades respond by freeing them by force.
Within weeks, fighting spreads along thousands of kilometres of railway.
The soldiers at the centre of it belong to the Czechoslovak Legion.
They are trying to cross Russia, and leave the country.
Instead, they will capture cities, and help transform the Russian Civil War.
Their own country... does not yet exist.
And when it finally does, many of them will still be stranded, on the other side of the world.
Four years earlier, these men had no national army to join.
The Czech lands belonged to the Austrian half of Austria-Hungary.
Slovakia was governed within the Hungarian half.
Their inhabitants were subjects of the Habsburg monarchy, and when the First World War began, many were called upon to fight for it.
But among Czechs and Slovaks abroad, some saw an opportunity.
If Austria-Hungary lost the war, its rulers might lose their grip on the peoples living beneath them.
Independence could become possible, provided the victorious powers supported it.
That support would have to be earned.
In Russia, Czech emigrants volunteered to fight against Austria-Hungary.
Their small formation initially served largely in reconnaissance, gathering intelligence and operating near enemy positions.
Recruiting from captured Austro-Hungarian soldiers gradually expanded its ranks.
A prisoner could now volunteer to fight against the empire whose uniform he had worn.
It offered a way out of captivity, but also a dangerous commitment.
Austria-Hungary regarded its citizens serving the enemy as traitors.
Capture could mean execution.
Meanwhile, independence leaders worked to turn military service into political influence.
Tomash Masaryk and his colleagues needed the Allies to see Czechs and Slovaks as partners capable of building a state.
An army fighting on their side gave that argument substance.
Every successful action offered evidence that their movement could contribute to victory.
But in nineteen seventeen, the Russian army around them began falling apart.
The tsar abdicated.
Years of casualties, shortages, and frustration had undermined military discipline.
Russia's new provisional government continued the war, even as increasing numbers of soldiers wanted it ended.
That summer, the Czechoslovak brigade received an opportunity to prove itself.
On July the second, at Zuh-borov, its troops broke through Austro-Hungarian positions,
and captured thousands of prisoners.
The wider Russian offensive failed.
The brigade's success nevertheless attracted attention, and helped open the way for further recruitment.
The force expanded into an army corps.
By the end of nineteen seventeen, it numbered nearly forty thousand volunteers.
Its leaders now possessed the military force they had wanted.
But they were about to lose the front on which it was supposed to fight.
The Bolsheviks seized power later that year, and moved to withdraw Russia from the war.
For the legionaries, peace between Russia and Germany solved nothing.
Austria-Hungary still existed.
Independence remained uncertain.
Their military usefulness depended on continuing the struggle alongside the Allies.
France offered a destination.
Getting there was the problem.
Moving west meant confronting territory controlled by the Central Powers.
Instead, the proposed route ran east, across Russia, to the Pacific port of Vladivostok.
From there, ships could transport the troops onward toward France.
The journey required moving an entire army across a country sliding into civil war.
For the moment, an agreement made that seem possible.
The legionaries would leave, surrendering most of their weapons while retaining a limited armed guard.
But the agreement rested on trust that neither side possessed.
Bolshevik authorities feared an armed force connected to the Allies travelling through their territory.
The legionaries feared becoming helpless, if local authorities stopped honouring their passage.
Weapons were concealed aboard their trains.
They began moving east, but slowly.
Their units became separated across vast distances.
Each delay left individual groups vulnerable, uncertain when the next train, or the next order, would arrive.
Then came the violence at Chelyabinsk.
The confrontation did not create the distrust.
It turned that distrust into armed resistance.
Orders for disarmament collided with the legionaries' determination to keep their weapons, and continue travelling.
Local clashes developed into a wider struggle.
Being scattered across Russia initially looked like a disaster.
No single position contained the whole Legion.
Units could be isolated and attacked separately.
Yet that same dispersal placed experienced soldiers near stations and junctions across an enormous railway network.
They began taking those positions.
To free a train, they needed a station.
To protect the station, they needed the surrounding approaches.
To reach another stranded unit, they needed the track between them.
Their escape route became a battlefield.
By the summer, Legion forces had helped seize major centres along the railway.
Anti-Bolshevik groups benefited from their advances, and established themselves where Soviet authority had been driven out.
A dispute over passage had become part of a struggle over who would govern Russia.
The railway explains how a comparatively small foreign army could matter so much.
Siberia was enormous.
Occupying every settlement across that territory was beyond the Legion's strength.
But controlling junctions and stations allowed troops to move, supplies to travel, and separated formations to support one another.
The trains carried the army's ability to keep fighting.
Lose a locomotive, a bridge, or a stretch of track, and the distance to safety could suddenly become impossible to cross.
This also explains why the legionaries could win battles without securing their departure.
Every advance created another position to defend.
Every connection restored became a route that could be cut again.
Their military success attracted powerful people who wanted them to stay.
Allied leaders saw a force capable of resisting the Bolsheviks, and potentially helping rebuild a front against Germany.
Assistance for the Legion became entangled with wider plans for intervention.
The men who wanted passage out of Russia were being treated as a reason to send other armies in.
Meanwhile, their reputation travelled much faster than their trains.
Abroad, the existence of Czechoslovak forces strengthened the independence movement's claim to represent a nation already contributing to the Allied war effort.
Diplomats could point to soldiers fighting under their movement's authority.
Their proposed country had an organised force before it possessed internationally established borders.
During nineteen eighteen, Allied recognition of the Czechoslovak leadership advanced.
Then Austria-Hungary began disintegrating.
On October the twenty-eighth, independence was proclaimed in Prague.
The political objective that had justified the Legion's existence had finally been achieved.
Czechoslovakia was becoming a state.
But that changed the meaning of every further casualty in Russia.
The men now had a homeland to return to.
Why should they continue dying so far away from it?
In November, the fighting on the Western Front ended.
The original plan, to cross Siberia and reach France before the world war was over, had been overtaken by events.
Yet an armistice in Europe could not move a stranded train.
Nor could a declaration in Prague remove the armed forces between the legionaries and Vladivostok.
They remained caught in Russia's struggle.
Their anti-Bolshevik partners were divided.
Allied promises and military assistance failed to produce the decisive results some had expected.
Exhaustion and losses weakened the Legion's willingness to keep fighting.
Its role increasingly shifted toward guarding the railway, and keeping traffic moving.
That sounded less demanding than a major offensive.
It still meant defending the narrow route on which their departure depended.
By nineteen nineteen, the country they had helped bring into existence was beginning its own political and military life.
Many of its celebrated soldiers remained abroad, protecting tracks through Siberia.
As the anti-Bolshevik armies suffered defeat, departure became more urgent.
Remaining in Russia meant risking further entanglement in a cause increasingly distant from their own.
The Legion needed arrangements that would allow its remaining formations to reach the coast.
In February, nineteen twenty, an agreement with Soviet authorities at Kooy-toon helped clear the way for their evacuation.
After years of changing commands, broken expectations, and fighting, the journey could finally move toward its end.
But reaching the ocean was only the last stage of their Russian ordeal.
Ships still had to carry them home.
Evacuation transports took soldiers and accompanying civilians out through Vladivostok.
The final legionary transport left in September, nineteen twenty, almost two years after Czechoslovakia declared independence.
Some men died, even during the sea journey.
Their graves joined those scattered along the routes the Legion had travelled.
The last evacuation transport reached Czechoslovak territory in November.
The distance between independence and homecoming had been measured in years.
The Legion's story is often remembered through its victories:
prisoners becoming soldiers,
soldiers capturing cities,
and an army surviving a journey across Russia.
But those victories carried a strange consequence.
The more useful the Legion became to other powers, the harder it became for its men to leave.
They had joined a war to help secure independence.
They had crossed into another war while trying to continue the first.
And after their country finally appeared on the map, they still had to negotiate and fight for the chance to reach it.
When the survivors returned, Czechoslovakia was no longer a political promise made by exiles abroad.
It was the place where they could finally step off the train.
